title_en: Notice of the Supreme People's Court on Issuing the First Batch of Guiding Cases
ruling_gist_en: The contractual provision in a house sale intermediary contract that prohibits the buyer from using the property information provided by the intermediary company to circumvent that intermediary and directly enter into a sale contract with the seller is legally valid and effective. However, when the seller lists the same property for sale through multiple intermediary companies, and the buyer obtains the same property information through other publicly available legitimate channels, the buyer has the right to choose an intermediary company with lower fees or better service to facilitate the conclusion of the house sale contract. In such circumstances, the buyer's actions do not constitute a breach of contract, as the buyer did not utilize the property information from the intermediary with which it previously contracted.
keywords_en: contract dispute; sales contract; house sale
full_text_en:
Supreme People's Court

Notice on Issuing the First Batch of Guiding Cases

Fa [2011] No. 354

To the High People's Courts of all provinces, autonomous regions, and municipalities directly under the Central Government, the Military Court of the People's Liberation Army, and the Production and Construction Corps Branch of the High People's Court of Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region:

In order to implement the Central Government's judicial reform measure of establishing a case guidance system, the Supreme People's Court issued the "Provisions on Case Guidance Work" (hereinafter referred to as the "Provisions") on November 26, 2010. The issuance of the "Provisions" marks the initial establishment of a case guidance system with Chinese characteristics. All sectors of society have paid close attention to this and have given strong support. In accordance with the requirements of the "Provisions," each High People's Court actively recommended and submitted guiding cases to the Supreme People's Court. The Supreme People's Court specifically established the Case Guidance Work Office to strengthen and coordinate research on guiding cases among relevant parties. Recently, the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court discussed and adopted, and decided to publish four cases, including Shanghai Zhongyuan Property Consulting Co., Ltd. v. Tao Dehua — dispute over an intermediary contract, as the first batch of guiding cases. The relevant work is hereby notified as follows:

I. Accurately Grasp the Guiding Spirit of the Cases

(1) The case Shanghai Zhongyuan Property Consulting Co., Ltd. v. Tao Dehua — dispute over an intermediary contract, aims to resolve disputes arising from a buyer "skipping the intermediary" in second-hand housing transactions. This case confirms: The stipulation in an intermediary contract that prohibits the buyer from using the property listing information provided by the intermediary company to bypass that intermediary company and sign a house sale contract with the seller is binding, meaning the buyer shall not breach the contract by "skipping the intermediary." However, if the same property listing information is published by multiple intermediary companies, and the buyer obtains such property listing information through legitimate channels, the buyer has the right to choose an intermediary company with a lower quotation and better service to facilitate the conclusion of the transaction; such conduct does not constitute a breach by "skipping the intermediary." This both protects the legitimate rights and interests of intermediary companies, promotes the healthy development of the intermediary service market, maintains the integrity of market transactions, and promotes fair competition among housing intermediary companies, improves service quality, and protects the legitimate rights and interests of consumers.

(2) The case Wu Mei v. Sichuan Meishan Xicheng Paper Co., Ltd. — dispute over a sales contract, aims to correctly handle the validity relationship between a settlement agreement reached outside litigation and a court judgment. This case confirms: Where parties reach a settlement agreement outside litigation during second instance and then withdraw the appeal, the parties shall perform in accordance with the agreement. If one party fails to perform or does not fully perform the settlement agreement, the other party may apply to the people's court for enforcement of the first instance judgment that has taken legal effect. This both respects the parties' right to freely dispose of the subject matter of the dispute, emphasizes the rule that agreements must be adhered to and performed, and maintains the authority of the effective judgments of the people's court.

(3) The case Pan Yumei and Chen Ning — bribery, aims to resolve the issue of identifying bribery crimes committed through new forms and means. This case confirms: Where a state functionary accepts bribes in the name of "jointly operating" a company or in the form of a transaction, accepts bribes by promising to "seek benefits for others" without actually seeking benefits, or returns the illicit gains to cover up the crime, such conduct does not affect the determination of bribery. This provides clear guidance for handling cases of accepting bribes through new means in recent years. It is of great significance for legally punishing bribery crimes, effectively investigating and dealing with new types of bribery cases emerging under the new circumstances, and promoting the in-depth development of the anti-corruption struggle.

(4) The case Wang Zhicai — intentional homicide, aims to clarify the specific conditions for imposing a death sentence with a reprieve and restricting commutation. This case confirms: The restriction on commutation system provided for in the Criminal Law Amendment (VIII) may apply to criminal acts committed before April 30, 2011; where the crime is extremely serious, and a death sentence with immediate execution should be imposed, and the victim's side has a strong reaction, but the defendant has statutory or discretionary mitigating circumstances, and imposing a death sentence with a reprieve while simultaneously deciding to restrict commutation can achieve proportionality between crime and punishment, a death sentence with a reprieve and restriction on commutation may be imposed. This is conducive to effectively implementing the criminal policy of combining leniency and strictness, both severely punishing serious criminal offenses in accordance with the law and further strictly restricting the death penalty, maximizing the increase of harmonious factors and minimizing discordant factors, and promoting the construction of a harmonious society.

II. Effectively Utilize the Role of Guiding Cases

People's courts at all levels shall organize judges to study and research the above guiding cases, deeply understand and correctly grasp the spiritual essence and guiding significance of the guiding cases; shall enhance the consciousness of applying guiding cases, strictly refer to the guiding cases to adjudicate similar cases with advanced judicial concepts, fair judgment standards, and scientific judgment methods, further improve the quality and efficiency of case handling, ensure the organic unity of the legal effect and social effect of judgments, and guarantee social harmony and stability; shall attach great importance to case guidance work, carefully compile and select, actively recommend, and promptly submit guiding cases, continuously improve the quality of selected and reported cases, and promote the solid development of case guidance work; shall give full play to the guiding role of public opinion, publicize the significance and effectiveness of the case guidance system, and create a good atmosphere for all sectors of society to understand, care about, and support the trial work of the people's court.

Hereafter, each High People's Court may guide the trial work of people's courts at all levels within its jurisdiction and special courts by issuing reference cases and other forms, but shall not use the terms "guiding case" or "guiding precedent" to avoid confusion with guiding cases. For issues encountered in implementing case guidance work and suggestions for improving case guidance work, please promptly report level by level to the Supreme People's Court.

Attachment: Four guiding cases including Shanghai Zhongyuan Property Consulting Co., Ltd. v. Tao Dehua — dispute over an intermediary contract

December 20, 2011

Guiding Case No. 1

Shanghai Zhongyuan Property Consulting Co., Ltd. v. Tao Dehua — dispute over an intermediary contract

(Adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, published on December 20, 2011)

Keywords: civil, intermediary contract, second-hand housing transaction, breach of contract

Ruling Gist

The stipulation in a housing transaction intermediary contract that prohibits the buyer from using the property listing information provided by the intermediary company to bypass that intermediary company and sign a house sale contract with the seller is legally valid. However, when the seller lists the same house for sale through multiple intermediary companies, and the buyer obtains the same property listing information through other legitimate channels that are accessible to the public, the buyer has the right to choose an intermediary company with a lower quotation and better service to facilitate the conclusion of the house sale contract. The buyer's conduct does not involve using the property listing information of the intermediary company with which it previously contracted, and therefore does not constitute a breach of contract.

Relevant Laws

Article 424 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China

Basic Facts

Plaintiff Shanghai Zhongyuan Property Consulting Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Zhongyuan Company) alleged: The defendant, Tao Dehua, used the sales information for a house located at No. X, Zhuzhou Road, Hongkou District, Shanghai, provided by Zhongyuan Company, intentionally bypassed the intermediary, and privately signed a house purchase contract directly with the seller, violating the terms of the "Real Estate Purchase Confirmation Letter" and constituting malicious "skipping of the intermediary" conduct. The plaintiff requested the court to order Tao Dehua to pay Zhongyuan Company liquidated damages of RMB 16,500 in accordance with the agreement.

Defendant Tao Dehua argued: The original owner of the house in question, Li Moumou, entrusted multiple intermediary companies to sell the house; Zhongyuan Company was not the exclusive holder of the property listing information and was not the exclusive agent for the sale. Tao Dehua did not use the information provided by Zhongyuan Company and there was no breach of contract for "skipping the intermediary."

The court found the following facts through trial: In the second half of 2008, the original owner, Li Moumou, listed the house in question for sale with several housing intermediary companies. On October 22, 2008, a Shanghai real estate brokerage company showed the house to Tao Dehua; on November 23, a Shanghai real estate consulting company (hereinafter referred to as a certain real estate consulting company) showed the house to Tao Dehua's wife, Cao Moumou; on November 27, Zhongyuan Company showed the house to Tao Dehua and signed the "Real Estate Purchase Confirmation Letter" with Tao Dehua on the same day. Clause 2.4 of the said "Confirmation Letter" stipulated that within six months after Tao Dehua inspected the real estate, if Tao Dehua or his client, agent, representative, undertaker, or any person related to Tao Dehua, using the information, opportunities, or other conditions provided by Zhongyuan Company, entered into a transaction with a third party without going through Zhongyuan Company, Tao Dehua shall pay liquidated damages to Zhongyuan Company at 1% of the actual transaction price reached with the seller regarding the real estate sale. At that time, Zhongyuan Company quoted the house at RMB 1.65 million, while a certain real estate consulting company quoted it at RMB 1.45 million and actively negotiated the price with the seller. On November 30, through the intermediation of a certain real estate consulting company, Tao Dehua signed a house sale contract with the seller at a transaction price of RMB 1.38 million. Later, the buyer and seller completed the transfer procedures, and Tao Dehua paid a commission of RMB 13,800 to a certain real estate consulting company.

Judgment

The Hongkou District People's Court of Shanghai rendered civil judgment (2009) Hong Min San (Min) Chu Zi No. 912 on June 23, 2009: Defendant Tao Dehua shall pay liquidated damages of RMB 13,800 to plaintiff Zhongyuan Company within ten days from the effective date of the judgment. After the judgment was announced, Tao Dehua appealed. The Shanghai No. 2 Intermediate People's Court rendered civil judgment (2009) Hu Er Zhong Min Er (Min) Zhong Zi No. 1508 on September 4, 2009: 1. Set aside the civil judgment (2009) Hong Min San (Min) Chu Zi No. 912 of the Hongkou District People's Court of Shanghai; 2. The claim of Zhongyuan Company requesting Tao Dehua to pay liquidated damages of RMB 16,500 is not supported.

Reasoning

The effective judgment of the court held that: The "Real Estate Purchase Confirmation Letter" signed between Zhongyuan Company and Tao Dehua is in the nature of an intermediary contract. The stipulation in Clause 2.4 is a standard term commonly found in housing transaction intermediary contracts that prohibits "skipping the intermediary." The intent is to prevent the buyer from using the property listing information provided by the intermediary company to "skip" the intermediary company and purchase the house, thereby preventing the intermediary company from receiving the commission it deserves. This stipulation does not involve circumstances such as exempting one party's liability, increasing the other party's liability, or excluding the other party's main rights, and shall be deemed valid. According to this clause, the key to determining whether the buyer has breached the contract by "skipping the intermediary" is whether the buyer has used the property listing information, opportunities, or other conditions provided by the intermediary company. If the buyer did not use the information, opportunities, or other conditions provided by the intermediary company but obtained the same property listing information through other legitimate channels accessible to the public, then the buyer has the right to choose an intermediary company with a lower quotation and better service to facilitate the conclusion of the house sale contract, and does not constitute a breach by "skipping the intermediary." In this case, the original owner listed the same house for sale through multiple intermediary companies. Tao Dehua and his family members learned of the same property listing information through different intermediary companies and facilitated the conclusion of the house sale contract through another intermediary company. Therefore, Tao Dehua did not use the information or opportunities provided by Zhongyuan Company, and thus did not constitute a breach of contract. The claim of Zhongyuan Company is not supported.

Guiding Case No. 2

Wu Mei v. Sichuan Meishan Xicheng Paper Co., Ltd. — dispute over a sales contract

(Adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, published on December 20, 2011)

Keywords: civil litigation, enforcement, settlement, withdrawal of appeal, non-performance of settlement agreement, application for enforcement of first instance judgment

Ruling Gist

During the second instance of a civil case, the parties reach a settlement agreement outside litigation, and the people's court grants permission to withdraw the appeal. If such settlement agreement has not been formally made into a mediation document by the people's court in accordance with the law, it is an agreement reached outside litigation. If one party fails to perform the settlement agreement, and the other party applies for enforcement of the first instance judgment, the people's court shall support such application.

Relevant Laws

Article 207, Paragraph 2 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China

Basic Facts

Plaintiff Wu Mei is the owner of Wu Mei Waste Collection Station in Dongpo District, Meishan City, Sichuan Province, engaged in the waste paper collection business. Starting around 2004, Wu Mei sold waste paper to the defendant, Sichuan Meishan Xicheng Paper Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Xicheng Paper Company). On April 14, 2009, the parties settled accounts, and Xicheng Paper Company issued an IOU to Wu Mei stating: "We owe Wu Mei waste paper payment of RMB 1,970,000 (￥1,970,000.00)." On June 11 of the same year, the parties again settled accounts for later payments, and Xicheng Paper Company issued an IOU to Wu Mei stating: "We owe Wu Mei waste paper payment of RMB 548,000 (￥548,000.00)." After repeated demands for payment of the above amounts were unsuccessful, Wu Mei filed a lawsuit with the Dongpo District People's Court of Meishan City, requesting the court to order Xicheng Paper Company to pay RMB 2.518 million in payment for goods plus interest. The defendant Xicheng Paper Company did not dispute owing Wu Mei RMB 2.518 million.

After trial, the first instance court rendered a judgment: The defendant Xicheng Paper Company shall pay the plaintiff Wu Mei RMB 2.518 million in payment for goods plus default interest within ten days from the effective date of the judgment. After the judgment was announced, Xicheng Paper Company appealed to the Meishan Intermediate People's Court. During the second instance proceedings, on October 15, 2009, Xicheng Paper Company signed a repayment agreement with Wu Mei, stipulating Xicheng Paper Company's repayment plan, and Wu Mei waived the claim for interest. On October 20 of the same year, Xicheng Paper Company applied to withdraw the appeal on the grounds of voluntarily reaching a settlement agreement with the other party. After the Meishan Intermediate People's Court ruled to grant permission to withdraw the appeal, because Xicheng Paper Company did not fully perform the settlement agreement, Wu Mei applied to the first instance court for enforcement of the first instance judgment. The Dongpo District People's Court of Meishan City supported Wu Mei's application for enforcement of the first instance judgment. Xicheng Paper Company applied to the Meishan Intermediate People's Court for enforcement supervision, requesting that the original first instance judgment not be enforced.

Judgment

The Meishan Intermediate People's Court issued a reply (2010) Mei Zhi Du Zi No. 4 on July 7, 2010, holding that: Based on Wu Mei's application, the first instance court accepted the enforcement of the effective legal document, which is not improper, and enforcement shall continue.

Reasoning

The court held that: Xicheng Paper Company should have known the legal consequences of withdrawing the appeal. That is, once the court ruled to grant its withdrawal of the appeal, the first instance judgment of the Dongpo District People's Court of Meishan City became a legally effective judgment with enforceable effect. Although the parties voluntarily reached a settlement agreement during the second instance that stipulated relevant rights and obligations, and Xicheng Paper Company gave up the right to appeal by signing the agreement, and Wu Mei waived interest, this settlement agreement is an agreement reached outside litigation by the parties. It was not confirmed by the people's court in accordance with the law to produce a mediation document, and therefore does not have compulsory enforcement effect. Xicheng Paper Company's failure to perform its repayment obligations under the settlement agreement violated the parties' agreement and the principle of good faith. Therefore, its request, based on the parties reaching a settlement agreement, that the original effective judgment should not be enforced is not supported.

Guiding Case No. 3

Pan Yumei and Chen Ning — bribery

(Adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, published on December 20, 2011)

Keywords: criminal, bribery, "jointly operated" company, bribery, purchasing house at low price, bribery, promise to seek benefits, calculation of bribery amount, concealing bribery by returning illicit gains

Ruling Gist

1. Where a state functionary takes advantage of his office to seek benefits for an entrusting person, and obtains "profits" in the name of "jointly operating" a company with the entrusting person without actual capital contribution and participation in management, it shall be dealt with as bribery.

2. Where a state functionary, knowing that an entrusting person has matters to request, accepts property from that person, it is deemed as a promise to "seek benefits for others." Whether benefits have actually been sought for others or obtained does not affect the determination of bribery.

3. Where a state functionary takes advantage of his office to seek benefits for an entrusting person, and purchases items such as a house from the entrusting person at a price obviously lower than the market price, it shall be dealt with as bribery. The amount of bribery is calculated based on the difference between the local market price at the time of the transaction and the actual price paid.

4. Where a state functionary, after accepting property, returns it to conceal the crime due to the investigation of persons or matters related to his bribery, this does not affect the determination of the crime of bribery.

Relevant Laws

Article 385, Paragraph 1 of the Criminal Law of the People's Republic of China

Basic Facts

Around August to September 2003, defendants Pan Yumei and Chen Ning took advantage of their positions as, respectively, Secretary of the Party Working Committee of Maigaoqiao Subdistrict, Qixia District, Nanjing, Jiangsu Province, and Director of the Maigaoqiao Subdistrict Office, to provide assistance to general manager Chen of a Nanjing real estate development company in obtaining 100 mu of land at a low price in the Maigaoqiao Entrepreneurship Park. On September 3, jointly with Chen, they registered and established Nanjing Duohe Industry and Trade Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Duohe Company) in the names of their relatives to "develop" the said land. Pan Yumei and Chen Ning neither made actual capital contributions nor participated in the company's management. In June 2004, Chen, in the name of Duohe Company, transferred the company and its land to a Nanjing sports goods company. Pan Yumei and Chen Ning, under the guise of participating in profit distribution, each received RMB 4.8 million from Chen. In March 2007, because Pan Yumei was under investigation, Chen Ning, while on a business trip in the United States, arranged for his driver to return RMB 800,000 to Chen. After the case was exposed, all illicit gains and proceeds from such gains obtained by Pan Yumei and Chen Ning were recovered in accordance with the law.

From February to October 2004, defendants Pan Yumei and Chen Ning took advantage of their positions as, respectively, Secretary of the Party Working Committee of Maigaoqiao Subdistrict and Director of the Maigaoqiao Subdistrict Office to provide assistance to a Nanjing real estate development company in purchasing land in the Maigaoqiao Entrepreneurship Park, and on four separate occasions each accepted RMB 500,000 from general manager Wu Moumou of that company.

In the first half of 2004, defendant Pan Yumei took advantage of her position as Secretary of the Party Working Committee of Maigaoqiao Subdistrict to provide assistance to a Nanjing development company in obtaining a reduction of RMB 1 million in fees for the assignment of the Jinqiao Building project, and when purchasing a property developed by that company, accepted over RMB 610,000 from general manager Xu Moumou of that company to cover the price difference and related taxes and fees (the price of the house including taxes and fees was RMB 1,210,817, and Pan paid RMB 600,000). In April 2006, because the procuratorial authority had learned from Xu's company's accounts that Pan had only paid part of the purchase price for the house, Pan repaid RMB 550,000 to Xu.

In addition, from before the 2000 Spring Festival to December 2006, defendant Pan Yumei took advantage of her position to successively accept RMB 2.01 million and USD 490,000 from Gao Moumou, a Party branch secretary of the Maigaoqiao Subdistrict Office and general manager of a Nanjing commercial trade company, and USD 10,000 from Fan Moumou of a Zhejiang real estate group's Nanjing company. From 2002 to 2005, defendant Chen Ning took advantage of his position to successively accept RMB 210,000 from Gao Moumou, a Party branch secretary of the Maigaoqiao Subdistrict Office, and RMB 80,000 from Liu, Deputy Director of the Maigaoqiao Subdistrict Office.

In summary, defendant Pan Yumei accepted bribes totaling over RMB 7.92 million and USD 500,000 (equivalent to RMB 3.981234 million), totaling over RMB 11.902 million; defendant Chen Ning accepted bribes totaling RMB 5.59 million.

Judgment

Nanjing Intermediate People's Court of Jiangsu Province rendered a criminal judgment (2008) Ning Xing Chu Zi No. 49 on February 25, 2009, finding that the defendant Pan Yumei was guilty of bribery and sentencing her to death, with a two-year suspension of execution, deprivation of political rights for life, and confiscation of all personal property; the defendant Chen Ning was guilty of bribery and sentenced to life imprisonment, deprivation of political rights for life, and confiscation of all personal property. After the judgment was pronounced, Pan Yumei and Chen Ning appealed. Shandong High People's Court rendered a criminal ruling (2009) Su Xing Er Zhong Zi No. 0028 on November 30, 2009, based on the same facts and reasoning, rejecting the appeal, affirming the original judgment, and approving the first-instance criminal judgment sentencing the defendant Pan Yumei to death, with a two-year suspension of execution, deprivation of political rights for life, and confiscation of all personal property for bribery.

Reasoning

The effective judgment of the court held: Regarding the defense opinion of the defendants Pan Yumei, Chen Ning, and their defense counsel that the "profit" of RMB 4.8 million obtained by the two defendants and Chen Mou from jointly establishing Duohe Company to develop land should not be considered as bribery. Upon investigation, at the time, Pan Yumei was the Party Committee Secretary of Maigaoqiao Subdistrict Office, and Chen Ning was the Director of Maigaoqiao Subdistrict Office. They both had the responsibility of leading or coordinating the investment attraction work and land transfer of Maigaoqiao Start-up Park. They each utilized their respective official positions to provide assistance for Chen Mou to obtain the land of the Start-up Park at a low price, which constitutes using official influence to seek benefits for others. During this period, Pan Yumei, Chen Ning, and Chen Mou discussed and agreed to jointly establish Duohe Company to develop the said land. The registered capital of the company all came from Chen Mou. Pan Yumei and Chen Ning neither made actual capital contributions nor participated in the company's operation and management. Therefore, the RMB 4.8 million each obtained by Pan Yumei and Chen Ning under the guise of jointly establishing a company with Chen Mou to develop the land was not so-called company profits, but rather a portion of the benefits obtained by using official influence to enable Chen Mou to acquire land at a low price and then resell it. This reflects the essence of an exchange of power for money in the crime of bribery, constituting a disguised form of bribery in the name of jointly establishing a company, and should be treated as bribery.

Regarding the defense opinion of defendant Pan Yumei and her defense counsel that Pan Yumei did not actually seek benefits for Xu Moumou. Upon investigation, when the petitioner Xu Moumou bribed Pan Yumei, he requested a reduction of RMB 1 million in fees when acquiring the Jinqiao Building project. Pan Yumei knew that Xu Moumou had a request matter but still accepted the bribe. Although the request matter was not fulfilled, "seeking benefits for others" includes different stages of conduct: promising, implementing, and realizing. Having only one of these constitutes seeking benefits for others. A promise to "seek benefits for others" can be determined from an express or implied expression of intent to seek benefits for others. Pan Yumei accepted property from Xu Moumou knowing that he had a request matter, which should be deemed as a promise to seek benefits for others. Whether benefits were actually sought or obtained for others is only a matter of the circumstances of the bribery and does not affect the determination of bribery.

Regarding the defense opinion of defendant Pan Yumei and her defense counsel that Pan Yumei's purchase of real estate from Xu Moumou should not be considered as bribery. Upon investigation, the market price of the real estate purchased by Pan Yumei, including taxes and fees, was a total of over RMB 1.21 million. Pan Yumei only paid RMB 600,000, which was significantly lower than the local market price at the time of the transaction. Pan Yumei used her official position to seek benefits for the petitioner and purchased real estate from the petitioner at a price significantly lower than the market price. This conduct is a means of covering up the essence of an exchange of power for money in bribery by formally paying a certain amount of consideration. It should be treated as bribery, with the bribery amount calculated based on the difference between the local market price at the time of the transaction and the actual payment.

Regarding the defense opinion of defendant Pan Yumei and her defense counsel that Pan Yumei purchased real estate developed by Xu Moumou and, before the case was discovered, had paid the price difference to Xu Moumou, so it should not be considered as bribery. Upon investigation, in April 2006, before the case was discovered, Pan Yumei paid RMB 550,000 to Xu Moumou as a supplement for the price difference on the real estate she had purchased from Xu Moumou's development. This was nearly two years after her low-price purchase in the first half of 2004, and she had not promptly repaid the huge price difference. Pan Yumei's supplementary payment was a voluntary surrender of illicit gains for the purpose of covering up her crime, after Xu Moumou had been called in for questioning by the procuratorial authority regarding another case and the procuratorial authority had learned from the accounts of Xu Moumou's company that Pan Yumei had only paid a portion of the purchase price for the real estate. Therefore, Pan Yumei's supplementary payment of the housing price difference to conceal her crime does not affect the determination of her bribery.

In summary, the above defense opinions raised by the defendants Pan Yumei, Chen Ning, and their defense counsel cannot be established and are not adopted. Pan Yumei and Chen Ning, as state functionaries, each utilized their respective official positions to seek benefits for others and accepted property from others. Their conduct constituted the crime of bribery, and the amount of bribes was particularly huge. However, considering that both defendants, after being brought to justice, truthfully confessed their crimes, showed a good attitude of admitting guilt, voluntarily confessed other crimes of the same nature that the judicial authorities had not yet discovered, returned part of the illicit gains before the case was discovered, and cooperated in the recovery of all the illicit gains involved after the case was discovered, they were given lighter punishment. Therefore, the first-instance and second-instance courts made the above judgments in accordance with the law.

Guiding Case No. 4

Wang Zhicai -- Intentional Homicide Case

(Adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, published on December 20, 2011)

Keywords: criminal; intentional homicide; triggered by love/marriage disputes; confession; remorse; death sentence with a two-year suspension of execution; restriction of commutation

Ruling Gist

In an intentional homicide case triggered by the intensification of love or marriage conflicts, if the defendant's criminal means are cruel and the crime warrants the death penalty, but the defendant has mitigating circumstances such as confession, remorse, and active compensation, and at the same time the victim's family demands severe punishment, the People's Court may, based on the nature of the case, the circumstances of the crime, the harmful consequences, and the defendant's subjective malignancy and personal danger, lawfully sentence the defendant to death, with a two-year suspension of execution, and at the same time decide to restrict commutation, in order to effectively resolve social conflicts and promote social harmony.

Relevant Legal Provisions

Article 50, paragraph 2 of the Criminal Law of the People's Republic of China

Basic Facts

The defendant Wang Zhicai and the victim Zhao Moumou (female, died at age 26) established a romantic relationship while they were classmates at Weifang Vocational College of Science and Technology in Shandong Province. In 2005, after Wang Zhicai graduated and started working, Zhao Moumou was admitted to Qufu Normal University in Shandong Province for a top-up bachelor's degree program. In 2007, after Zhao Moumou graduated and started working, Wang Zhicai discussed marriage with Zhao Moumou. Because Zhao Moumou's family disagreed, Zhao Moumou repeatedly proposed breaking up, but the two continued to keep in touch at Wang Zhicai's insistence. At noon on October 9, 2008, Wang Zhicai again discussed the relationship issue in Zhao Moumou's collective dormitory. When Zhao Moumou clearly stated that the two could not be together, Wang Zhicai felt desperate and angrily formed the intention to kill Zhao Moumou and then commit suicide. He then picked up a single-edged pointed knife in Zhao Moumou's dormitory and stabbed her repeatedly in the neck, chest, abdomen, and back, causing her to die from hemorrhagic shock. At approximately 8:30 a.m. the next day, Wang Zhicai attempted suicide by drinking pesticide but failed, and was captured by the public security authorities. Wang Zhicai usually behaved well. After being brought to justice, he truthfully confessed his crimes and actively compensated together with his relatives, but did not reach a compensation agreement with the victim's family.

Judgment

Weifang Intermediate People's Court of Shandong Province rendered a criminal judgment (2009) Wei Xing Yi Chu Zi No. 35 on October 14, 2009, finding that the defendant Wang Zhicai was guilty of intentional homicide and sentencing him to death, with deprivation of political rights for life. After the judgment was pronounced, Wang Zhicai appealed. Shandong High People's Court rendered a criminal ruling (2010) Lu Xing Si Zhong Zi No. 2 on June 18, 2010, rejecting the appeal, affirming the original judgment, and reporting the case to the Supreme People's Court for approval in accordance with the law. The Supreme People's Court, based on the facts confirmed upon review, rendered a criminal ruling (2010) Xing San Fu 22651920 Hao, disapproving the death penalty for the defendant Wang Zhicai and remanding the case to Shandong High People's Court for retrial. After retrial in accordance with the law, Shandong High People's Court rendered a criminal judgment (2010) Lu Xing Si Zhong Zi No. 2-1 on May 3, 2011, amending the sentence of the defendant Wang Zhicai for intentional homicide to death, with a two-year suspension of execution, deprivation of political rights for life, and at the same time decided to restrict commutation.

Reasoning

Shandong High People's Court held upon retrial: The conduct of the defendant Wang Zhicai constituted the crime of intentional homicide, and the crime was extremely serious, warranting the death penalty. Given that the case was triggered by a love dispute, Wang Zhicai became angry and formed the intention to kill after his marriage proposal was rejected, and after being brought to justice he confessed and showed remorse, actively compensated the victim's family for economic losses, and usually behaved well, he could be sentenced to death without immediate execution. However, considering that Wang Zhicai's means of intentional homicide were particularly cruel, the victim's family did not forgive him and demanded strict punishment in accordance with the law, in order to effectively resolve social conflicts, in accordance with Article 50, paragraph 2 of the Criminal Law of the People's Republic of China and other provisions, the defendant Wang Zhicai was sentenced to death, with a two-year suspension of execution, and at the same time it was decided to restrict commutation.
